title: Engine scheduling by column generation
contribution: Solves short-term switching-engine scheduling at in-plant railroads exactly via pattern concatenation, a set-partitioning master proven stronger than the compact MIP, and price-and-branch with a pattern-based labeling pricing algorithm using dual-bound label fathoming, plus a Ch. 2 column-generation synthesis and Ch. 6 theory on restricted PD paths (pp. 167-168).
problem_entry: BMBF industrial project on switching engines at steel-mill in-plant railroads (pp. 6, 13-14); entry via mismatch: m-PDPTW too general, practice uses only simple patterns (pp. 29, 31, 33); ESP strongly NP-complete (Def. 1.6, Lemmas 1.7-1.8, p. 32).
key_idea: Pattern concatenation (Lemma 1.3, p. 30) gives a set-partitioning master over concatenations (pp. 92-94) solved by column generation; pricing labels extend whole patterns with new dual-bound fathoming (pp. 116-124); price-and-branch for integers (pp. 128, 131).
assumptions: Binary set-partitioning master with convexity row per engine (pp. 92-93); deterministic data, ~2h requests certain (p. 20), integral times (p. 108), request-disjoint concatenations (p. 30); data vps real shift, eko with synthetic windows, eko80x hard, Sol's 80 instances (pp. 137-138).
proof_devices: strong NP-completeness by restriction from m-TSPTW (Lemma 1.7, p. 32)
fractional solution with weight 1/|E| giving trivial LP bound (Lemma 3.2, pp. 90-91)
Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition of compact LP to compare bounds (Lemma 3.3, pp. 93-94)
bound chain LB <= z* < 0 for gamma guarantee (Lemma 4.12, p. 127)
counting by induction and Stirling's formula (Lemmas 6.4-6.9, pp. 153-156)
path surgery on a line under triangle inequality, tight factor 3 (Prop. 6.12, p. 158)
expansion of Balas's layered graph (Thm 6.15, Cor. 6.16, pp. 160-163)
experiments: Pentium III, CPLEX 7.0, research prototype (p. 136); vps ladder, vps40 33-setting sweep, eko, eko80x, Sol's instances (Tables 5.3-5.10, pp. 141-148); baselines: own code without label elimination (orders of magnitude, p. 141), Sol's optima with differences named (pp. 143, 147), compact MIP only on vps10 (p. 149); failures and gaps kept, run-time profile (pp. 141-145); no seeds or statistics.
positioning: Continues Montreal school labeling/pricing (pp. 107-116, 38, 129); priority claims hedged with credit to Mehrotra & Trick and Mehlhorn & Ziegelmann (pp. 13, 32, 122-123); direct reasoned criticism of Kim & Nazareth and Boucher & Smeers (pp. 76-77).
writing: Chapter epigraphs, 'All claims ... are proved' (p. 6), hedged priority claims (pp. 13, 32, 123), concluding remarks naming gaps (pp. 57-58, 73, 84, 149, 164); candid Ch. 5 vs firmer summary claims (pp. 168, 192 against pp. 143, 145).
limits_future: Exact pricing bottleneck, request disjointness, no dual-choice advice, no branch-and-price, no polyhedral study, deterministic only (pp. 169-170); missing time-window data and practicability unshown (p. 149); future: hybrid labeling, dual cutting planes (p. 169), irregular pattern families, TSP cases (p. 164).

method_links.note: Compact model stated first and shown weak by proof, DW set partitioning proven stronger, pricing MIP rejected; but compact model judged by proof not measured, its one run an aside on smallest instance under another objective; no tree written, reasons integrality and branching compatibility.
Hard and synthetic sets to show failure, per-component ablation, failures and gaps kept, literature comparison names non-identical conditions, claim sized as research prototype.
Sizing slips in summary chapters: §7.2 generalises excellent vps bound to all problems against Ch. 5 gaps; compact-MIP comparison not identical; no variability protocol (Tension 3).
Ch. 2 synthesis with no new results but better relations, dual view organising, gaps named; own unstable duals as step 1; bibliography contributes in its own right; title returns in 2005 survey.
33-setting sweep read for trends, small-n counts as indication, proofs for restricted classes and conjecture; exit B without exit A.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: vps10 to vps50 ladder from one real shift.

transferable: Kill a compact big-M model on paper before running it: construct the fractional solution in which every engine serves every concatenation with weight 1/|E| and show that the LP relaxation attains only the trivial bound (Lemma 3.2, pp. 90–91).
Compare the LP bounds of two formulations by Dantzig–Wolfe-decomposing the compact LP and mapping each extensive solution into it (Lemma 3.3, pp. 93–94).

Fathom labels in a pricing DP with a dual bound: the best label cost at a state minus the positive duals of requests still admissible, compared with min(0, incumbent); tighten it with sets of mutually incompatible requests (pp. 121–124), and report run times with the bound switched off (Table 5.3, p. 141).
Turn an exact pruning test into a pricing heuristic with a guarantee: scale the bound by γ in (0, 1] and prove a relative error of at most 1 − γ (Lemma 4.12, p. 127).

Layer the column generators: column pool, then a greedy ranking by dual value over time-window slack, then the exact DP stopped at the k-th negative column, then the full exact DP only to prove optimality (Alg. 5.2, pp. 133–135).

Make every algorithmic component a command-line switch, print the defaults, and publish a sweep of the switches on one instance with integer value, gap, time and memory (Tables 5.1 and 5.4, pp. 130, 142).
Build a size ladder from one real instance by chronological truncation (vps10 to vps50) and mark runs beyond a stated cap, one CPU week, with a sign (pp. 137, 141).
Add a run-time profile by subroutine to locate the bottleneck (Table 5.7, p. 145).

When a literature benchmark uses another model, compute its objective from your solutions, tabulate both with their ratio, and name each difference (objective, horizon, path structure) in the text (pp. 143, 147).

Price a structural restriction with a tight worst-case factor: under the triangle inequality, place the optimal path on a line and repair interrupted patterns, traversing no segment more than three times; give the tight example (Prop. 6.12, p. 158).
For deployment: deliver a heuristic schedule at once, improve it with exact methods in the background, treat the output as a suggestion and never overrule manually fixed parts (p. 167).
